families.s: HSE scalding and burning controls for vulnerable people
families.t: bathing, showers, whole-body immersion, 44 C water, radiators, hot pipes, 43 C surfaces, legionella balance and maintenance
f: Vulnerable people in hospitals, care homes, special schools and supported housing may be at risk of scalding or burning.
Fatal scalding incidents have commonly occurred during bathing or showering.
Where vulnerable people are at risk during whole-body immersion, water temperature should not exceed 44°C.
Scald controls should not create additional risks such as legionella growth.
Hot pipes and radiators have caused serious and fatal contact burns.
Where vulnerable people may contact hot surfaces, HSE advises that the surface should not exceed 43°C at maximum design output.
Insulation or suitable guards can reduce contact with hot surfaces.
Risk assessment should cover residents' vulnerability, access, supervision, temperature control and equipment maintenance.
families.g: Scald and burn risk depends on vulnerability, water and surface temperature, exposure duration, bathing method, thermostatic controls, legionella controls, maintenance and supervision.

families.s: HSE control of nitrous-oxide exposure in maternity units
families.t: COSHH, gas and air, WEL, demand valves, scavenging, ventilation, monitoring, competence, pregnancy and maintenance
f: Nitrous oxide is an invisible anaesthetic gas subject to COSHH.
High exposure can cause neurological effects and anaemia through interference with vitamin B12.
The long-term workplace exposure limit is 100 ppm over an 8-hour time-weighted average.
Each space where nitrous oxide is used should have a COSHH exposure assessment.
A demand valve and mouthpiece or mask that captures exhaled breath is the most effective of the listed control systems.
Local scavenging or extraction near the patient's breathing zone can reduce release into the room.
General ventilation alone is the least effective listed control and normally needs evidence that adequate control is achieved.
Control systems require maintenance, user training and competent interpretation of exposure-monitoring data.
families.g: Nitrous-oxide risk depends on use pattern and demand, room and ventilation, capture and scavenging, worker proximity and shift pattern, maintenance, monitoring, pregnancy and competence.

families.s: HSE safe handling of cytotoxic drugs in healthcare and community settings
families.t: preparation, administration, waste, transport, spills, closed systems, extraction, PPE, hygiene, monitoring and training
f: Cytotoxic drugs can present significant occupational risks because they are toxic to cells.
Exposure can occur through skin contact or absorption, inhalation, ingestion and needlestick injuries.
Risk-generating activities include preparation, administration, patient waste, transport, disposal and spill cleaning.
COSHH requires employers to assess risks to employees and others affected by the work.
Totally enclosed systems should be used where reasonably practicable.
Exposure should be controlled at source using extraction and organisational measures before relying on PPE alone.
Safe handling, storage, transport, hygiene and contaminated-waste arrangements are required.
Workers need suitable information, instruction and training, including spill and contamination procedures.
families.g: Cytotoxic-drug risk depends on drug and formulation, preparation and administration method, contamination and waste, enclosure and extraction, exposure route, PPE, pregnancy and competence.

families.s: HSE control of diathermy and surgical-smoke emissions
families.t: electrosurgery, toxic gases, particles, vapours, respiratory effects, procedure, source capture, LEV, on-tip extraction and maintenance
f: Diathermy uses electric current to cut tissue or seal bleeding vessels.
Diathermy emissions can contain toxic gases, particles and vapours.
The emissions are often invisible to the naked eye.
Inhalation can adversely affect the respiratory system of theatre staff.
Risk varies with the procedure, equipment, environment, technique and patient.
COSHH requires assessment of risks from hazardous substances.
Exposure should be prevented at source where possible.
Where prevention is not possible, effective local exhaust ventilation, often on-tip extraction, is the usual control.
families.g: Surgical-smoke risk depends on procedure and tissue, energy device and technique, plume generation, room ventilation, source-capture position, exposure duration, maintenance and staff proximity.

families.s: HSE prevention and surveillance of dermatitis in health and social care
families.t: wet work, chemicals, physical and biological agents, sensitisation, gloves, skin care, early reporting, surveillance and assessment
f: Contact dermatitis is the most common work-related skin disease among nurses and other care professionals.
HSE estimates that around 1000 nurses develop work-related contact dermatitis each year.
Irritant dermatitis can result from wet work, chemicals, and physical or biological agents.
Allergic dermatitis can result from sensitising chemicals.
Employers should complete suitable and sufficient risk assessments.
Controls should reduce direct exposure and unnecessary wet work.
Health surveillance is appropriate where there is a residual risk of occupational dermatitis.
Early identification of itching, redness, cracking or blistering should trigger review and intervention.
families.g: Healthcare dermatitis risk depends on wet work, chemical and biological contact, glove use, hand hygiene, exposure duration, skin susceptibility, surveillance and early control review.
